title: Pauri 6, sound: teerath naavaa

segments.voice: Yesterday, visar, and the one Giver of pauri five. Your line was may I not forget. Did you remember who gave you something you used today? Day one hundred seventy-three.

At Haridwar on the Ganges, people step down the ghats at dawn into cold water. Other rivers and lakes draw people too, someone come to wash off a hard year. The janamsakhis, the old stories of Guru Nanak's life, say he walked to places like these. The sixth pauri of Japji opens on the riverbank, with a line about bathing. And its first line rings: two words that rhyme, side by side, like two feet stepping into water.
screen: `STEPS DOWN INTO A RIVER.` → `WASHING OFF A HARD YEAR.` → `TWO WORDS THAT RHYME.`

segments.voice: The opening line: teerath naavaa, je tis bhaavaa. Let's sound it. Teerath: TEE-rath. A teerath is a pilgrimage place, a holy ford, a spot on a river where people bathe. Naavaa: NAA-vaa, I would bathe. Je: jay, if. Tis: tiss, to Him. Bhaavaa: BHAA-vaa, I were pleasing. So you can hear it: I would bathe at the holy place, if I were pleasing to Him. And listen to the rhyme: naavaa, bhaavaa. The two halves of the line land on the same sound, like an echo. Then the line goes on: vin bhaane ki naae karee. Vin: without. Bhaane: pleasing. Ki: what. Naae karee: bathing would I do. Without pleasing Him, what bathing would I do? We'll open that tomorrow. Today, notice the music. Guru Nanak builds this pauri from rhyme and repetition, easy to carry in your head. And it has more of those sounds as it goes. There's a line with a string of treasures in it: ratan, javaahar, maanik, jewels, gems and rubies; you can hear their weight just in the sound. And then, again, the refrain you met in pauri five: guraa ik dehi bujhaaee. O Guru, give me this one understanding. When a refrain repeats, it's telling you what to hold onto. Two pauris in a row end on the same request. By now you might know it by heart. Say it in the practice if you do.
screen: `TEERATH — A HOLY FORD.` · `NAAVAA, BHAAVAA — A RHYME.` · `RATAN, JAVAAHAR, MAANIK.` · `THE REFRAIN COMES BACK.` · then, large: `PAURI SIX.`

segments.voice: Say the first line with me, slowly, out loud if you can. Teerath naavaa. Je tis bhaavaa. Again, and let the rhyme ring: naavaa, bhaavaa. Teerath naavaa. Je tis bhaavaa. Once more, softly. Then, if you can, add the refrain from pauri five: guraa ik dehi bujhaaee. Then sit. Picture cool water around your feet, and just breathe. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Ratan. A jewel: one of the treasures, ratan, javaahar, maanik, that ring through this pauri's sound, which opens teerath naavaa, I would bathe at the holy place.
Your line: teerath naavaa. Next time you wash your face or your hands today, say the line once, slowly, while the water runs. Day one hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: The sixth pauri of Japji is recited each morning; like the fifth, it ends with the refrain asking the Guru for one understanding, that there is one Giver of all.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the opening of Japji's sixth pauri, Ang 2.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about bathing.
what it means: I would bathe at the holy place, if I were pleasing to Him: the bath depends on the pleasing.
what a scholar hears: teerath is Sanskrit tirtha, a ford or crossing place, the same word behind the Jain tirthankara, a ford-maker.

notes: Teerath from Sanskrit tirtha (ford); tirthankara as 'ford-maker' in the trapdoor. Confirm.
Hook mentions Haridwar and Guru Nanak's visits to pilgrimage places as 'the stories say' (janamsakhi tradition). Confirm and check tone toward Hindu pilgrimage.
Romanization of 'vin bhaane ke naae karee': confirm.
